subject: [Prop Digest] Savills says no recovery until 2028
opener: Mortgage rates are up, forecasts are down, and the Bank of England is apparently thinking about changing the mortgage rules. Grab a coffee, this one's a slog.

stories.text: Savills expects average prices to drift lower for the rest of 2026, then fall 1.5% in 2027. Its reasoning is the Middle East war, which keeps mortgage rates higher for longer and makes buyers nervous. **Why it matters:** this is a forecast, not a fact, but it's a big agency-adjacent voice pushing back on the 'spring bounce' talk. If you're pricing stock or budgeting for a 2027 sale, assume it's a slow grind.
stories.headline: Savills says house prices won't recover until 2028

stories.text: The Bank of England is considering relaxing mortgage lending rules, according to Property Industry EYE. The summary is thin, so the detail is still to come. **Why it matters:** looser lending rules would widen the buyer pool, but only if the detail is real. Watch the fine print.
stories.headline: Bank of England may loosen mortgage lending rules

stories.text: Rent increases of up to 88% are still being approved in England, despite the Renters' Rights Act. Tenant challenges are at record levels since the Act came in in May, and both sides say the tribunal system is 'not working for anyone'. **Why it matters:** the Act was meant to curb unfair rises. If tribunals keep waving big jumps through, the tenant-friendly headlines won't mean much on the ground.
stories.headline: Rent rises of up to 88% still getting through

stories.text: Connells research says half of flats and two-thirds of new-builds sold last year would have been eligible under the First Homes price caps. **Why it matters:** if the caps cover most of the new-build stock, the scheme is less a niche policy and more a mainstream one. Developers and first-time buyers will both be paying attention.
stories.headline: Half of flats sold last year would have qualified for First Homes caps

stories.text: Rathbones' Charlie Newsome says property owners could see Income Tax bills rise by more than £1,000. **Why it matters:** with landlord tax changes already stacking up, this adds to the reasons some landlords are heading for the exit.
stories.headline: Landlords could face a tax bill jump of over £1,000

stories.text: Borrowing costs have reached a three-year high ahead of the Bank Rate decision, yet major lenders are cutting selected mortgage rates. **Why it matters:** the headline is bad, but the cuts show lenders fighting for the buyers who are left. Check the product, not the headline.
stories.headline: Mortgage rates hit a three-year high, but some lenders are cutting

stories.text: Foxtons saw opposition to key votes at its AGM on dividends and share allocation, and has responded. The summary doesn't say how the votes went. **Why it matters:** this follows the earlier shareholder backlash, so it's a pattern rather than a one-off.
stories.headline: Foxtons faces shareholder opposition at AGM

stories.text: Zoopla says one in three homes listed for sale were tracked on the portal before they hit the market, and its homeowner audience has reached 6.4m. This is the portal's own claim. **Why it matters:** if it's true, Zoopla is getting people to watch before they sell. That's a powerful pitch to agents, whatever the methodology.
stories.headline: Zoopla claims one in three listed homes was tracked first

stories.text: UK build-to-rent construction starts have fallen 63% in a year, with regional starts down 78%. **Why it matters:** fewer new rental homes means more pressure on rents in the years ahead.
stories.headline: Build-to-rent starts plunge 63%
Revolut froze a couple's account in a 'routine security review', and their £37,000 deposit is stuck with it. Nightmare timing with completion coming up.
